episode.title: Top US trade official reveals ‘problem’ in UK negotiations
episode.description:
The US trade representative says the UK is choosing the EU over America and Deutsche Bank organised almost $1bn of loans to a Hollywood studio landlord now in default. Plus, Nvidia has agreed to buy AI model platform Hugging Face for $13bn, and a look at how chicken became the world’s favourite protein.


Mentioned in this podcast:

UK-EU alignment is ‘problem’ for US trade deal, says top Trump official

Deutsche Bank led $1bn of troubled lending to Hollywood studio landlord

Nvidia to buy open-source AI platform Hugging Face for $13bn

Hugging Face attack is a wake-up call about the risks of AI

utterances.text: Good morning from the Financial Times. Today is Friday, September 4th, and this is your FT News Briefing. I'm Sonia Hudson in for Mark Filipino, and here's the news you need to start your day. Washington and London struck an initial trade agreement last year, but US Trade Representative Jameson Greer told the FT's Amy Williams that alignment with Brussels has been a sticking point in further negotiations. Deutsche Bank is dealing with some troubled loans. The German lender organized almost $1 billion worth of financing to a Hollywood studio landlord that's now defaulting. That's according to public court records and people familiar with the matter. The landlord is a private equity group called Hackmann Capital Partners, and it used the loans to buy 3 movie studios, 2 in Los Angeles and 1 in New York. But now all 3 of them are in default or foreclosure proceedings. Hackman was betting that the growth of Netflix, Amazon, and other streaming platforms would permanently boost demand for film and TV production space, but that bet did not pay off. Higher interest rates have made it harder to refinance the loans, plus film and TV production in LA has fallen sharply since actors' and writers' strikes a few years ago. Hackmann did not respond to a request for comment, and Deutsche declined to comment. NVIDIA is gaining more control over the AI industry. Yesterday, the chip giant agreed to buy the open-source AI model platform Hugging Face for $13 billion. It's NVIDIA's latest step to use its multi-trillion-dollar market cap to accelerate the AI boom, but it's also a wake-up call about the risks that come with it. Joining me now from San Francisco to discuss is the FT's Richard Waters. Hi, Richard.

utterances.speaker: F
utterances.text: Hi, great to talk to you.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: Great to have you on the show. So NVIDIA has had its eye on Hugging Face for a while. What does acquiring this company mean for NVIDIA's business going forward?

utterances.speaker: F
utterances.text: Well, Hugging Face is this extremely interesting community, if you like, community of developers in the center of the AI industry. All of these developers post their code there. They go there to find code that they can develop. It spans lots of different companies, lots of different people, and it's not the kind of thing that a big company normally owns. So NVIDIA is thinking, we want to become ourselves a bigger developer of AI models. We want them all to use our technologies. So let's try and own this community. Let's bring these developers into our orbit.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: Okay, NVIDIA's main business is chips, so AI hardware. Now it's buying this company that involves the software side of things. What concerns are people raising with this?

utterances.speaker: F
utterances.text: You've actually hit on what is a really central question here. There are 18 million developers who use Hugging Face. They use all kinds of technologies. They use different tools from different companies to develop their work. NVIDIA has a really difficult balancing act because on the one hand, it would love for all of these people to adopt NVIDIA technologies. They can become part of its ecosystem. They can develop on its chips. However, if it were to try to do that, it would cause a storm in the industry. It's exactly what happened nearly 10 years ago. When Microsoft bought GitHub. Back then, GitHub was the biggest online code repository, something very similar. And the entire world of developers said, hang on a minute, we don't want Microsoft stampeding in and squeezing us all into its technology ecosystem. And that's exactly where we are with NVIDIA.

utterances.speaker: B

utterances.text: Well, I think, you know, that touches on whether there will be antitrust questions here. There are echoes here of a few years ago when Nvidia tried to buy Arm, the chip design company, and that caused a real storm in the chip industry. Antitrust regulators ended up blocking that. But I think this time around it shouldn't be a problem from a regulatory point of view. This is a vertical deal. It's Nvidia moving into a different part of the AI system. So I think from a regulatory point of view, it should slip through, but that doesn't mean it's not going to face some really tough questions.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: Yeah. What are some of those questions?

utterances.text: I think the question for NVIDIA is how it uses its current very strong position to build a broader footprint across the AI world in the future. So the question, as always with a successful tech company at the moment, is how do they translate their current tech dominance, their current amazing cash flow into a good, strong competitive position in the next iteration of the industry. And that's what we're seeing NVIDIA try to do.
